speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Today, about 40% of our greenhouse gas emissions are attributed to electricity consumption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Through long-term planning, Singapore has built up a resilient and diversified energy supply through our "four switches" approach to facilitate our net zero and energy transitions – solar energy, regional power grids, low-carbon alternatives and natural gas – whilst decarbonising our energy mix.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Even as we pursue low-carbon alternatives, natural gas will remain Singapore's primary energy source for the foreseeable future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We will deploy advanced combined cycle gas turbine facilities to improve generation efficiency, lower our carbon footprint and support energy resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Energy efficiency continues to be a key enabler of our energy transition and an important way to strengthen energy security and cost competitiveness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: As a small and alternative-energy disadvantaged country, Singapore imports nearly all our energy supply and we must make every joule of energy count.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: According to the International Energy Agency, Singapore's energy intensity, which is the ratio of energy consumption to economic output, improved by 39% between 2000 and 2023.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The Middle East conflict has further reinforced the critical importance of energy resilience amid economic uncertainty, trade frictions and geopolitical conflicts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Gan highlighted in his Ministerial Statement on the Middle East Conflict earlier today, this crisis has exposed vulnerabilities in global energy supply chains and underscored the importance of a diversified and resilient power supply for our economy and our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: With rising energy demands and disrupted energy supplies, we must seize opportunities to decarbonise, reduce energy usage and conserve electricity by adopting more energy efficient practices and equipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This allows households, businesses and industries to reap cost savings and to do more with less.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The MEPS, the performance standards, and MELS, the energy labelling, under the Energy Conservation Act are key regulatory tools to enhance the energy efficiency of common, energy-intensive equipment, such as refrigerators, air-conditioners, motors and commercial storage refrigerators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These regulations were introduced in 2009 to regulate the local supply of such regulated goods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The MEPS aim to raise the average energy efficiency of regulated goods in Singapore by removing the least energy efficient models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Under the MELS, local suppliers are required to affix energy labels on regulated goods, which enable customers to compare energy efficiencies and savings across models and make more informed purchasing decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: One is a set of performance standards for the equipment, the other is a mandatory labelling scheme to make sure consumers are informed about the performance standards of the equipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: To enhance energy efficiencies across sectors, regulatory coverage has progressively expanded from three types of regulated goods in 2009 to eight today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Commercial storage refrigerators and water heaters were the most recent additions in April 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This approach has significantly increased the market share of more energy-efficient appliances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The Energy Conservation Act currently regulates importers, manufacturers and suppliers that provide the local sale and supply of regulated goods, with non-compliance carrying fines of up to $10,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: However, similar goods that are directly imported by end users, such as businesses and households, for their own use are not covered under the Energy Conservation Act today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The current volume of such imports may be small, but this could increase over time as online marketplaces have made it increasingly easy for consumers to import such goods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Some businesses are already directly importing commercial storage refrigerators for their own use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: First, this leads to the uneven application of MEPS and MELS regulations on regulated goods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Currently, only regulated goods from local suppliers face compliance requirements while those imported for own use are not covered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Second, the purchase of imported regulated goods that are energy inefficient and do not comply with MEPS and MELS could lock businesses and households into higher life-cycle energy costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Energy efficient appliances might have a higher upfront cost but typically offer lower life-cycle costs through energy savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: For example, the life-cycle costs of MEPS-compliant commercial storage refrigerators are on average 30% lower than non-compliant models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The adoption of energy inefficient equipment reduces cost savings for consumers and leads to lower abatement outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We have already taken some administrative steps to address this regulatory gap.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Since 2023, the National Environment Agency (NEA) has collaborated with online platforms, like Lazada and Shopee, to voluntarily remove listings of non-compliant regulated goods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Nonetheless, given growing trends of importing regulated goods for one's own use, regulatory levers are needed to ensure such goods comply with MEPS and MELS requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: End users would be required to ensure that regulated goods brought into Singapore for own use are registered with NEA, meet MEPS in accordance with prescribed international test standards and test conditions, and are labelled with the required energy labels under MELS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The proposed regulations exclude second-hand or used regulated goods where it is impractical to assess MEPS compliance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These compliance requirements are not expected to be onerous for end users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: While local suppliers pay a one-time registration fee of approximately $70 per model of regulated good, this will be waived for end users who typically cannot spread registration costs across multiple units.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: To demonstrate MEPS and MELS compliance, end users can rely on test reports from overseas suppliers and manufacturers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This would achieve a comparable cost of compliance between end users and local suppliers at approximately $1 per unit of regulated good.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The compliance requirements will extend to all regulated goods imported for own use, except regulated lamps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This is consistent with existing penalties in the Energy Conservation Act for the local supply of non-compliant regulated goods and the import of non-compliant greenhouse gas goods for own use in the Environmental Protection and Management Act 1999.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The proposed amendments to the Energy Conservation Act will also empower the Minister to make regulations to compel online platforms in Singapore or with a business establishment in Singapore to remove non-compliant listings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This will ensure that non-compliant products are not offered to end users in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: NEA will conduct systematic monitoring of online platforms and spot checks for non-compliance as needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: NEA will also conduct investigations in response to whistle-blowing reports or complaints and leverage existing powers in the Energy Conservation Act to enforce compliance with the new regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: To adjust to these regulatory changes, businesses and households can continue to leverage existing Government schemes to offset higher upfront costs of energy efficient regulated goods and realise energy savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This Grant covers up to 70% of costs for pre-approved energy efficient regulated goods, such as three-tick refrigerators and five-tick air-conditioning units to help businesses improve energy efficiency outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Singaporean and Permanent Resident Housing and Development Board (HDB) Households as well as Singapore Citizen households living in private residential properties can use $400 of Climate Vouchers under the enhanced Climate Friendly Households Programme to purchase eligible energy efficient regulated goods.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Iran War is affecting our energy supply and our daily lives – rising petrol and diesel prices and higher electricity prices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In fact, if the war prolongs, the supply of fuel and electricity may have to be rationed too, which is already happening in our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is a stark reminder that we must conserve energy to the best we can and use energy-efficient equipment and appliances in our industries, in our factories and in our homes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Over the years, as business practices evolved and consumers import equipment and appliances direct from foreign original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) or wholesalers, there is a growing volume of imported electrical appliances being used by end users in businesses and in households which may be non-energy efficient.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These direct imports are usually significantly cheaper than regulated goods sold by local suppliers, because of the removal of a layer of middleman cost.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Most end users buy these imported goods to save money upfront – they may not care about energy efficiency or longer-term higher electricity prices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: A local catering business owner told me that he imports refrigerators, chillers and freezers directly from OEMs because of the lower prices, which can be 60% to 70% cheaper than similar models sold by local suppliers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These appliances typically last only around 1.5 to two years, while reputable brands with higher energy efficiency from local supplies may last longer, around two to 2.5 years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Overall, we will see more efficient appliances on the market soon – not because of this amendment Bill but because of the global energy crisis.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: OEMs will be motivated to produce energy efficient models because end users will care about both upfront capital expenses and recurring electricity costs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The outcome of this amendment is that end users will have more choices of energy-efficient models as well as savings both in capital expenses and recurring electricity costs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I do have two questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The amendment Bill would empower NEA to take action against businesses and households which import non-compliant regulated goods.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In the food and beverage (F&B) sector alone, there were 6,355 registered restaurants as of 2023.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This figure would be a lot higher if we include the broader F&B sector, such as cafes, bars, food courts, hawker stalls and other specialised food services.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Also, there is a high churn in this industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In 2024, close to 3,000 restaurants closed down while nearly 3,800 new food and restaurant businesses opened.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Given the large number of F&B businesses, coupled with the short average lifespan of two to three years for refrigerators, chillers and freezers, does NEA have an estimate of the total number of electrical appliances and equipment that may be procured annually, as well as the total annual energy consumption?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With the amendment Bill, what is the projected reduction in energy consumption, should all F&B businesses deploy MEPS- and MELS-compliant appliances and equipment?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I hope the process and requirements will not be too onerous both for the NEA enforcement team and on the part of end users.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We should not want to conserve energy in one form, only to expend it in another form.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Bill requires end users who import regulated electrical products for personal or commercial use to register these appliances with the National Environment Agency (NEA) and demonstrate compliance with Minimum Energy Performance Standards (MEPS), thereby closing the regulatory gap where such imports were previously unregulated.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: NEA will be granted enforcement powers to take action against non-compliance.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The global energy crisis will drive manufacturers to produce more energy-efficient models, thereby benefiting end users who can save on both initial costs and ongoing electricity expenses.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Singapore households can achieve dual savings by combining Government-provided climate vouchers with the direct import of efficient appliances from overseas suppliers, whilst business operators, particularly those in the food and beverage industry who need to purchase multiple appliances, can also avoid excessive energy costs by using energy-efficient models.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This amendment aims to strike a balance between cost savings and environmental responsibility.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, the key to achieving energy conservation lies in implementing these new regulations in an efficient and effective manner.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Otherwise, we would merely be conserving energy in one form whilst consuming more human resources in another. : Mr Deputy Speaker, it is important that we do what is right for the environment, especially at this time of threatened energy supplies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Climate change is an existential threat to our island nation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As I argued during the Budget debate in February, our transition to net zero must be backed by rigorous effective action that is both technically sound and socially just.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must ensure that our green ambitions do not inevitably place an unfair burden on our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and lower-income citizens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While we must prevent the entry of energy-guzzling appliances into our market, we must consider the SME squeeze in the e-commerce space.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Unlike large multinational corporations with dedicated compliance departments, our local SME retailers often lack the resources to navigate complex technical test reports for every niche product they list.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If a listing is flagged and digitally removed due to a documentation error or a delay in NEA registration, the loss of sales momentum and search algorithm ranking can be devastating for a small business.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will there be a grace period or a simplified verification pathway for local micro-enterprises to ensure they are not crowded out of the digital marketplace by larger players with deeper pockets for compliance?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, ambiguity in the circumvention threshold for consumers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This Bill expends the act to cover goods imported for own use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While this certainly closes a loophole for traders, it creates a grey area for individual consumers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many Singaporeans often sell items on online platforms, like Carousell, that are almost brand new, perhaps a gift they cannot use, or a high-end appliance bought for a renovation that was later aborted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have three specific clarifications for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Are all listings on peer-to-peer sites, like Carousell, now subject to these digital removal laws?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If so, how will the NEA distinguish between a genuine second-hand sale by a resident and a commercial trader masquerading as individual to offload non-compliant stock?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What criteria will NEA officers use to prove deliberate evasion versus a genuine change of mind?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Without clear guidelines, we risk a situation where an innocent individual selling a gift is caught under the same heavy penalty framework as a rogue trader.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How does the Bill apply to those who receive an imported appliance as a gift and wish to sell it?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must ensure that our drive for energy efficiency does not inevitably criminalise the legitimate second-hand gift economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are certifying the physical engine but ignoring the digital driver.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am concerned that the Bill remains silent on software-driven energy degradation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is a growing risk that a product's registered efficiency, the very basis of its NEA approval, can be remotely altered post-purchase.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Manufacturers can push over-the-air updates that cap performance to protect hardware longevity at the expense of efficiency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In a Tesla battery litigation in the United States, linked to the 2019 Hong Kong incident, Rasmussen against Tesla 2021 and the 2024 Norwegian Court of Appeal case, we saw disputes over allegations that over-the-air updates throttled capacity and charging speeds to manage hardware longevity post-sale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If an industrial battery or EV charger is registered at a certain efficiency, but a firmware update throttles it six months later, the original registration becomes a moot point.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Companies, like ABB, now offer an energy optimisation as a service.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These AI-driven systems predict load demands for industrial motors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, how do we prevent the possible scenario that the hardware may revert to a high consumption baseline mode if a local SME stop paying the subscription, even though the physical hardware is perfectly capable of running efficiently?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must ensure that energy efficiency is not held hostage by software subscriptions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The US Department of Energy found that heating ventilation and air conditioning systems often prioritise warranty protection over energy savings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If a chiller software detects a minor sensor error, it may default to a mechanical safety mode that consumes 30% to 40% more energy without alerting the owner.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This silent degradation means a building's energy audit may look good on paper, but the software is secretly wasting power.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The proposed amendment in this Bill seeks to encompass own use, imports and digital advertising within the regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, the absence of specific projections regarding expected energy savings or carbon abatement from these suggested additions prevent Parliament and Singaporeans from being able to value the efficacy of these measures or account for their performance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, there is a lack of clarity regarding whether the administrative burdens and cost placed upon the public and SMEs are truly proportionate to the actual carbon reductions achieved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the Bill closes existing regulatory gaps, could the Senior Minister of State provide the specific annual energy conservation targets the Government expects to meet through these new own-use and advertising measures?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And what methodology will the NEA employ to track and report these savings to the public?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am also concerned that the Bill's restrictions on own use e-commerce imports may inadvertently raise the entry price for essential appliances.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While high efficiency models offer long-term savings, the upfront green premium may potentially create a financial barrier for lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must ensure that these regulations do not unfairly burden those who are currently relying on budget-friendly direct imports.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, technical and financial barriers of SME compliance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Unlike large retailers who spread these costs over thousands of units, small enterprises face a "compliance tax" that creates a literal barrier to modernisation as such.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Without a simplified registration pathway, the potentially high cost and complexity of compliance may pervert the Bill's intent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Local firms may find it cheaper to keep older, less efficient machinery in operation longer, rather than navigating the new regulatory hurdles to import updated high efficiency technology.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the NEA recognises test report for Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA)-accredited labs, the actual data submission for single unit imports remains administratively heavy for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a move would ensure that compliance costs do not inevitably discourage our local enterprises from adopting the latest energy-saving technologies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, addressing the exclusion of high frequency goods like lighting.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the Ministry has prioritised larger appliances like refrigerators and chillers for the own-use import regime, it has specifically excluded lighting for the time being.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, the cumulative energy footprint of inefficient lighting imported via direct e-commerce remains significant.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A phased approach that leaves out these high frequency items may allow a continued influx of sub-standard bulbs and tubes, which may undermine our overarching goal of reducing aggregate household demand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What is the specific data driven justification for excluding lighting from own-use import regulations at this stage?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, can the Senior Minister of State provide a definitive timeline or road map for when these and other low consumption but high frequency goods will be included to prevent a prolonged regulatory vacuum?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, while this Bill closes necessary retail loopholes, we must not lose sight of the bigger picture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Since 2013, our most energy-intensive facilities have been tracking data under this Act, yet for a number of years, the needle on actual efficiency may not have moved much.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the debate for the second reading of the 2017 amendments for the Energy Conservation Act, the then-Minister for the Environment and Water Resources, Mr Masagos Zulkifli, noted that while Energy Conservation Act companies saw efficiency gains of 0.4% and 0.6% in 2014 and 2015 respectively, meeting our climate pledge requires doubling or tripling these rates to 1% to 2% annually, in order to match then-leaders like Belgium and the Netherlands.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the 2017 amendments introduced mandatory management systems and audits, they seem to have stopped short of requiring companies to actually implement these energy saving opportunities they identified, provided they met the MEPS for their equipment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And is the Ministry confident that the incremental system-by-system mandates will hit our 2030 targets in time?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, the Workers' Party supports the intent of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Climate change is an existential threat to Singapore, but in pursuing net-zero goals, we must also balance policy fairness and transparency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I worry that the new "digital deletion" requirements and complex registration procedures will be a "compliance tax" for small businesses with limited resources.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government should provide a "fast track" or simplified procedures and not let cumbersome paperwork hinder businesses from adopting energy-efficient technology.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many residents sell unused appliances or gifts on websites like Carousell.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If the legal definitions are unclear, might ordinary citizens become "illegal suppliers" for selling a "non-compliant" gift?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many appliances today have their efficiency controlled by software.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If manufacturers reduce energy-saving effectiveness through remote updates after selling products or revert devices to high-energy consumption mode because users have not paid software subscription fees, then the original energy-saving registration becomes meaningless.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, in conclusion, the Workers' Party believes in a green transition defined by transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must implement changes in this Bill with operational integrity and adjust transition protections that our people and our SMEs deserve.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications that I have sought, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I support the Bill because it closes a gap in our energy efficiency framework.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: To ensure this amendment works in practice, there are three areas that we must get right.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: First, ensuring clarity on who bears responsibility and how the requisite standards can be met.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In practice, end-users, such as SMEs, often operate through layered procurement arrangements and may not realise they are legally treated as the importer, even when they did not control the purchase.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Second, ensuring adequate support for SMEs to transition.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Compliance can be costly for SMEs, given that upfront costs for non-compliance are often lower.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In many cases, household purchases are occasional and more straightforward, as consumers often turn to trusted local suppliers who have already registered these appliances and ensured that they meet prevailing standards.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The compliance risks are likely to be more acute for businesses, in particular SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Unlike larger corporations, many SMEs do not have dedicated procurement, legal or compliance teams to check whether the goods they are bringing in meet Singapore's regulatory requirements.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Their decisions are often driven by cost, speed and availability, and are frequently made through contractors, franchisors, fit-out firms or overseas suppliers.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: There are at least three scenarios where an SME may inadvertently fall foul of the rules.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: First, an SME setting up a new outlet may engage a contractor to source the necessary appliances.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In trying to keep costs low and meet timelines, the contractor may purchase these goods from an overseas online platform without checking whether they comply with Singapore's MEPS and MELS requirements.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Second, a franchisee may purchase equipment specified by the brand owner, in order to maintain consistency with the wider franchise network or may have a contractual obligation to purchase such equipment.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: A franchisee may assume that because the equipment is approved or offered by the franchisor, it is also compliant with Singapore's regulatory standards.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Third, many SMEs rely on interior designers or contractors to deliver a unit on a turnkey basis.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Appliances, such as refrigeration units, water heaters or air-conditioning systems may be imported as part of the fit-out package, and the SME owner may not even realise that they are also, in legal terms, treated as the importer responsible for compliance.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In each of these scenarios, the SMEs may not have controlled the procurement decision, but may still bear the responsibility as the importer.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Unlike larger corporations, the SMEs may not have the bargaining power to either transfer compliance obligations or enforce standards on third-party vendors.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For that reason, while this Bill affects both individuals and businesses, it has greater practical impact on local businesses, and I would like to focus my remarks mainly on SMEs and on how importer liability will be determined in practice.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is perhaps helpful to start by understanding the scale of the problem that the new laws seek to address.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In particular, it would be useful to understand how significant this gap has become and why it is important to address it at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: And what factors drove the need for the amendment at this point in time?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is also helpful to understand the feedback that went into shaping the proposed new laws.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Could the Ministry clarify whether SMEs, platform operators and other intermediaries in the procurement chain were also consulted, and how their views were taken into account?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This brings me to my concerns about compliance and enforcement – that is, whether and how SMEs will comply with the Act, and whether and how NEA will actively enforce this new offence.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In principle, I appreciate that businesses operating in Singapore should know that they must comply with Singapore laws.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In an ideal world, all consumers and businesses would check before purchasing and importing regulated goods.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, as explained earlier, that is not how many SMEs actually buy equipment.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Take the example of a franchisee in the F&B sector who is told to purchase a standard set of equipment from the franchisor.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Where the franchisee chooses to move ahead with the purchase, it could be a case of reasonably assuming or relying on third-party assurances that the equipment is compliant; not having enough bargaining power to convince the franchisor to switch; or making an informed, commercial decision that this may fall foul of the regulations.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If it makes more commercial sense for SMEs to risk non-compliance with the Act, then the amendment may not achieve its intended deterrent effect.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: First, there are the cost-savings of imported versus non-imported goods.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: That is a substantial difference for a single unit, and even more so for bulk purchases.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In many cases, the headline cost of regulated goods from overseas sources or parallel imports can be significantly lower.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Second, there are also further indirect costs which may accompany compliance.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Where a company or person intends to import a regulated good for their own use, they must still produce test reports to demonstrate that the goods are compliant with the relevant standards.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, where the brand is less known or where the manufacturer's in-house laboratory testing is not to the required standards, the business owner would bear the responsibility of sourcing private lab testing, which can be very costly, both in terms of time and costs.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Lab tests lead time and costs could potentially result in commercial delays of months, and cost businesses thousands of dollars.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Whether one is a contractor, fit-out firm or end-user, there is often little immediate incentive to choose the more expensive piece of equipment.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Yet, these appliances also have long operating lives, which means that once a non-compliant equipment enters the market, it may remain in use for many years.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This makes the NEA's task of education and enforcement significantly more challenging.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: One may argue that the long-term energy savings from more efficient equipment should make commercial sense.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But that is not always immediately apparent to SMEs that are managing day-to-day operational pressures, cashflow constraints and tight set-up budgets.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While larger firms may be able to absorb these compliance costs, SMEs may instead treat the risk of non-compliance as part of their start-up considerations.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: More importantly, has NEA considered how these factors may shape business behaviour, including whether some SMEs may treat the risk of non-compliance as part of their set-up considerations?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In addition, will the NEA consider publishing a public list of commonly used equipment that are compliant, their cost relative to non-compliant equipment and the estimated lifetime energy cost savings?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This serves two purposes: empowering and educating the public to make informed decisions and incentivising upstream suppliers to ensure that their equipment are compliant.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Moving on from compliance, I would like to ask about NEA's plans for enforcement.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The issue of who bears responsibility as the importer is particularly important when we consider how enforcement will operate in practice.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If penalties are to shape behaviour, they must be understood in practice and calibrated relative to the upfront savings from non-compliant equipment.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Enforcement should follow a clear sequence – closing the information gap, supporting compliance and then applying firm penalties.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Given that much of the current risk appears to arise from information gaps and layered procurement arrangements, I hope the Government will consider a stronger transition approach.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This could include broader consultation and outreach, a temporary transition or regularisation window, and where appropriate, expedited support for SMEs that are willing to switch to compliant and more energy-efficient equipment.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, schemes, such as the Energy Efficiency Grant play an important role in supporting SMEs in this transition.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In practice, an SME's decision may change when the support quantum and scope are taken into account, particularly if audit and reimbursement processes do not place pressure on immediate cash flows.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I would therefore suggest that such schemes can be further streamlined or enhanced to support affected SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I note that Senior Minister of State, Finance, has already expanded this Energy Efficiency Grant to all sectors today.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I would encourage the Ministry to consider further expanding Energy Efficiency Grant's scope to cover all regulated goods.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, this Bill serves Singapore’s goals of meeting our climate targets and paves our path for sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Energy efficiency is a quiet but important part of energy policy.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is about managing Singapore’s electricity demand and strengthening our resilience to external energy shocks.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Amidst ongoing geopolitical uncertainties and volatility in global energy markets, improving energy efficiency becomes even more important.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Every unit of electricity we save reduces exposure to external energy shocks and builds towards our energy resilience.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, I believe that this must also be balanced against the impact of regulations on the people.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is not sufficient for us to rely on regulations and expect the people to meet our energy efficiency goals.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, I wish to seek several clarifications from the Senior Minister of State on the enforcement architecture, the scope of Director-General's new powers and the question of interagency coordination, particularly between the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE), which oversees the industry and household sectors under this Act and the Ministry of Transport (MOT), which oversees the transport sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It goes to the heart of whether these amendments will have practical effect.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For commercial shipments, our existing regulatory infrastructure is well established.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: TradeNet declarations, licensed warehouses and customs checkpoints provide natural interception points, but the own use imports targeted by this Bill arrive through very different channels.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Consider the practical scenarios: a person orders a portable air-conditioning unit from an overseas e-commerce platform, and it arrives via international parcel post.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A business owner drives across the Causeway with a piece of industrial equipment in the back of a van; a traveller returns from a trip with a new kitchen appliance in checked baggage.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In none of these cases is there an obvious regulatory checkpoint at which compliance can be verified.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: That framework already provides the certifying matters relating to the import of goods and includes a provision allowing the Minister to prescribe additional certifiable methods.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Energy efficiency compliance could be prescribed as one such matter, allowing importers of regulated goods to declare compliance through an existing system that Singapore Customs and traders are already familiar with.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, for goods arriving by post or courier, will the Ministry be working with Singapore Customs and Singapore Post to establish screening protocols.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Will parcel manifest or trade description be used to flag potential non-compliant imports?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, for goods brought in by land through the checkpoints, what role will the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) play?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Is it realistic to expect ICA officers, whose primary focus is immigration and security, to also screen for energy efficiency compliance?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Fourth, will enforcement be proactive through inspections and spot checks or reactive, relying on complaints and tip-offs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: If the latter, the Bill's deterrent effect may be significantly limited.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Without a credible enforcement framework, we risk creating a prohibition that exists on paper but is widely disregarded in practice.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: That outcome would undermine public confidence in the regulatory regime and create unfairness within compliant importers who bear the cost of registration and those who simply do not bother.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Bill also grants the Director-General broad discretion under section 31B to grant or refuse waivers, based on whether there are good reasons to do so.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that the Bill includes procedural safeguards.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Director-General must give written notice of proposed conditions or modifications and allow registration holder to make written representations before a decision is made.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: There is also an appeal mechanism to the Minister under section 17.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, I wish to raise several points on the adequacy of these safeguards.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, the powers to impose or modify conditions at any time is very broad.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: There is no requirement that conditions be related to the original purpose of the registration, no cap on the frequency of modifications and no requirement that conditions be proportionate.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, the Bill does not specify any timeframe within which the registration holder must be given to make representations.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This is left entirely to the Director-General's discretion.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This Bill, by contrast, sets no such minimum.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, on a waiver mechanism under section 31B.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The criterion of good reason is inherently subjective.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I will ask the Senior Minister of State whether the Ministry intends to publish guidelines, setting out the circumstances in which waivers will typically be considered, so that applicants have reasonably certainty and the regime is applied consistently across cases.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Fourth, will decisions of the Director-General, particularly refusals of waivers and impositions of conditions, be published or reported in any aggregated form.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Transparency in decision making is essential to maintaining public and industry confidence in the regulatory regime.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Energy Conservation Act is jointly administered by MSE, which oversees the industry and household sectors, and MOT, which oversees the transport sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This Bill's expansion to cover own use imports will necessarily engage many more Government agencies beyond this existing arrangement.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Enforcement at the border will require the active cooperation of Singapore Customs for commercial and postal shipments, the ICA for goods brought in at the land and air checkpoints and potentially, the Info-communications Media Development Authority for enforcement against online platforms and digital advertisements.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For the industrial sector, there will also be a need for coordination with the Economic Development Board, which promotes industrial investment and the Energy Market Authority, which oversees broader energy sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Where a regulated good falls under both the household and transport sectors, for example, an electric vehicle charger imported for personal use, it is not immediately clear whether the importers' obligations fall under MSE's or MOT's purview, or both.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Bill itself does not address inter-agency coordination.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I note, however, that the Bill's closing statement declares that it will not involve the Government in any extra financial expenditure.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: That is difficult to comprehend with the substantial new administrative functions these amendments introduce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: My concerns are not with the Bill's objectives but with the practical details that will determine whether these amendments work on the ground, how we enforce at the border and how we safeguard against unchecked discretionary powers and how we coordinate across the many agencies involved.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I look forward to the Senior Minister of State's response to these points.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding my queries and clarifications, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Strengthening energy efficiency remains an important pillar in Singapore's energy transition.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is not new, because since 2012, our approach rested on two sensible ideas.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, to set minimum standards for energy performance; and second, to help consumers, like you and I, with clearer information through energy labelling so that households and businesses can make better purchasing decisions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I would like to raise four broad concerns.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, the ordinary layperson does not think of himself or herself as an importer when they purchase goods from overseas to Singapore.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, the current user journey to register makes it difficult for those who are not confident in English.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, I wonder whether if it is time to review the volume of information on the energy label.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My first point is about how we secure support and buy-in of individual customers or consumers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Under this Bill, a person who imports certain regulated goods for his or her own use will have to grapple with the framework that was previously once used for commercial supply lines into Singapore's market.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I note that during a public consultation, one suggestion was to require end users, which is consumers, like myself, to buy goods only from local suppliers since local suppliers may be better place to handle compliance requirements.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Government did not take that route, and I think that is sensible.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should preserve consumer choice so long as compliance framework applies consistently.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In the same vein, my remarks pertain mainly to ensure that reporting and compliance regime is workable and understandable for the ordinary consumer.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The ordinary layperson does not think of himself or herself as an importer, in any formal sense.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To many, they are simply just thinking they are making a purchase.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially so because some Singaporeans do cross over the Causeway to buy household appliances because of lower prices.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some might even organise trips with their friends across the causeway to shop for items for their Build-To-Order flats.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In such cases, such consumers are unlikely to perceive themselves as importing a regulated goods, subjecting to registration or compliance requirement in the first instance.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, in this regard, I would like to ask how the Ministry intends to communicate these requirements to the public.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In responding to how, I am keen to understand how various personas have been considered.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As a matter of fact, not every Singapore resident will be following this view, or even looking at this response that I am making, and many might not even realise that if they make purchase of certain regulated goods from overseas for their own use, there might be a need for registration or compliance requirement that applies to them.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But again, such mechanism only helps if a person knows that it exists, understands what it may be applied to and knows how to register.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This brings me to my second point, which is the accessibility of user journey.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I know this may sound operational, but operational details matter because they shape whether people comply easily or give up along the way.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If the registration journey is mainly online, then we should think carefully about who are likely the users.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While some might be comfortable using their smartphones, not all will be fully comfortable navigating an English-only or English-heavy website.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: There are those who are not deterred by the policy itself, but because of the number of steps they have to go through, they give up halfway.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And I am sure most of us at some point in our life would have experienced this because you have to fin so many steps or do many things.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Halfway, you decide you do not want to continue that journey of application.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In short, what I am really trying to say is that have we designed this portal with various personas in mind?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, questions worth asking: can the process be made simpler?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Can there be automatic reminders or notification if renewal is required for certain registration?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Furthermore, some of our residents who are not digitally savvy, might purchase non-bulky instantaneous water heater or mini refrigerator from overseas as part of their shopping.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Would there be a possibility that they can register in person simply because they are not digitally confident?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If so, could MSE or NEA share what would the process look like?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This will go a long way in enabling businesses and individuals to comply with more robust reporting more seamlessly.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: You see, in policy design, reducing friction is not a soft issue.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is part of what makes policy workable.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If we want wider compliance, then the process must be intuitive and low friction as possible.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When you buy the fridge from Best Denki, that sticker that you see.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This familiar tick has served important purpose by making energy efficiency more visible to consumers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But I think it is also fair to ask whether the current presentation remains useful and usable as it should be, and whether there should be further improvement moving forward.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I understand in my observation of various stickers, there are at least 10 sets of information in practice and what consumers first notice are the ticks.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Other information might be valuable, for example, annual energy consumption or estimated cost.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But I also wonder for those that have very small font size, whether these information are equally important in influencing purchasing decision?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, against this backdrop, I would like to ask the Ministry whether it has reviewed how consumers actually interpret such labelling and perhaps consider a more robust means of understanding what people focus on when they look at the label.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, questions to ask ourselves would be these: what information do they notice?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: More broadly, what is the behavioural objective of the label today?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Is it to mainly to help the uncle and auntie who is wondering around Best Denki or Gain City, to nudge them towards a higher efficiency option within that compliant range?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If so, do we really need at least 10 sets of information on that sticker?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This matters because the label is only effective, it is not only just rich in information, but it should be useful in helping to shape decision.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is why I also appreciate that NEA has started its clarification with some of the online platforms on the implementation concerns, but there are additional pointers that I would like to raise.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, what type of platforms would likely be covered?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, in the case where a platform holds large volumes of listing, what level of what levels of monitoring and due diligence will be expected of them, and what guidance or support might be provided for them so that they would comply easily?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These question matters because the line between platform responsibility, seller's responsibility and practical enforceability can be complex.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should want a regime that is effective, but also clear and proportionate.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But if we want this framework to work well, we must pay attention to the last mile.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should not only set sound legal rules, but also make compliance straightforward and simple for ordinary users.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should not only raise standards, but we should also make it easy for people to understand and what is expected of them.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should not only regulate for digital age, but also must ensure that implementation is practical for consumers, businesses and platforms alike.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If we get this balance right, we will make it easier for people to support Singapore's energy transition.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Conflicts, such as the Iran War, shows how quickly supply and prices can be disrupted.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For Singapore, with no natural resources and heavy reliance on energy imports, that risk is real and immediate.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I also speak from experience working in an energy generation firm.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Every day, we push to produce energy more efficiently and in ways that are cleaner and more cost effective.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Previously in this House, I raised concerns about water loss, because every drop counts.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Against this backdrop, this Bill is timely and necessary.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It strengthens one of the most practical levers we have – using less energy and using it more efficiently.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It ensures that rules apply across the board.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It prevents regulatory arbitrage and it creates a fairer, more level playing field while achieving the end goal.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This strengthens the regulatory regime by giving the Director-General powers to impose or modify conditions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In a fast-moving technological landscape, this flexibility is important.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Standards must evolve and new evidence must be acted upon.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If advertisements mislead, consumers cannot make informed choices.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If they are accurate, they reinforce the policy intent.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This provision helps align consumer behaviour with our energy goals.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Firms, especially SMEs, may need to upgrade equipment or change processes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While I appreciate that the overall life-cycle cost is potentially lower, there are real, upfront costs.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Can the Ministry elaborate on whether there will be more targeted support, transitional assistance, or differentiated timelines beyond the current scheme for smaller firms?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We should avoid a situation where the burden falls disproportionately on those least able to bear it, especially in this business climate.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Higher compliance costs may be passed on to consumers, and this is a real risk.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At a time of cost pressures, households will feel this.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And if substantial, how does the Ministry intend to mitigate this and ensure that the transition remains fair and inclusive?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Yes, clause 7 gives flexibility, but flexibility can also create uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Can the Ministry provide greater clarity as to when will conditions be modified, and will there be notice periods or consultation?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Greater predictability will give businesses the confidence to invest and comply.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But if we do nothing, what does that number become?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And what would that mean for our overall energy efficiency outcomes?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Understanding this trajectory will help us assess the scale and urgency of the problem.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It strengthens enforcement and it reinforces the importance of efficiency.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must manage the short-term impact on businesses.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And we must provide clarity to those affected.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we get this balance right, we will do more than just improve efficiency.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And we will move forward together towards a more sustainable future where everyone plays a part because in the end, this is not just about regulation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is about using what we have wisely, efficiently and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, I spoke with a SME owner in the logistics industry about the impact of recent energy price fluctuations on business operations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: He told me that whilst rising fuel prices do indeed increase costs, he was more concerned about something else – if energy supply becomes unstable, businesses might not even be able to obtain the energy needed for basic operations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, in an era full of geopolitical uncertainty, the greatest risk businesses face is often not merely price increases, but the possibility that operations could be forced to halt once supply is disrupted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This reminds us that, for Singapore, energy issues are not merely about pricing but are fundamentally related to national resilience, stable business operations and long-term economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As an old saying goes: "Prepare for rainy days to ensure steady progress." In today's constantly changing global energy landscape, improving energy efficiency is itself an important way to strengthen national resilience.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Energy efficiency remains one of Singapore's most pragmatic and cost-effective approaches to strengthening energy security and fulfilling climate commitments.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As a highly urbanised country with limited land and resources, Singapore depends on imports for over 95% of its energy.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, energy-related activities are also the main source of our nation's carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This means that every unit of energy we save not only reduces emissions, but also reduces dependence on imported energy, thereby enhancing overall national resilience.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, closing regulatory gaps to ensure consistent rules.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Previously, if businesses sell equipment, they have to comply with energy efficiency standards but if they directly import equipment for their own use, in certain circumstances, they might not necessarily be fully covered by the original regulatory system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is like a competition where some people enter through the main gate whilst others slip in through a side entrance.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Ultimately, those who follow the rules end up at a disadvantage and the system loses credibility.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This helps ensure all companies compete under the same rules and maintains market fairness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill further refines the registration system for regulated products.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Importers or manufacturers must complete registration procedures when supplying or importing relevant equipment and ensure products meet energy efficiency requirements.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If we compare the energy efficiency system to traffic rules, then the registration system is like vehicle registration.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Only by clearly knowing what equipment is in use and who introduced it to the market can regulatory authorities ensure rules are implemented.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, even the best standards would be difficult to enforce without clear registration and regulatory mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, driving businesses to continuously improve energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Equipment considered efficient 10 years ago may no longer be the best choice today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, some older air conditioning systems or industrial equipment can often significantly reduce energy consumption whilst lowering operating costs through technological updates or operational optimisation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: From a business point of view, this is quite easy to understand.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For the same type of equipment, some operate more efficiently whilst others are clearly more power-hungry.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Over time, the difference becomes not just a technical issue but a real cost difference.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: By strengthening the regulatory framework, this Bill encourages businesses to regularly review equipment and systems and gradually adopt more efficient technologies.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Speaker, energy efficiency is not merely an environmental responsibility but also an economic opportunity.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For businesses, energy is often one of the important operating costs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Improving energy efficiency can reduce costs, enhance productivity and reduce enterprise risk when facing international energy price fluctuations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With the world gradually moving towards a low-carbon economy, energy efficiency will also become an important factor in companies’ international competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, improving energy efficiency both aligns with sustainable development goals and helps strengthen economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Speaker, whilst I support the direction of this Bill, I would also like to raise three questions and suggestions for the government's consideration.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, if two companies use similar equipment, one completes registration according to regulations and ensures compliance with energy efficiency standards whilst another imports equipment through different channels without truly being covered by regulation, then the rule-abiding company actually bears higher compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In the long run, this not only undermines system credibility but also affects market fairness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, I suggest the Government consider strengthening spot checks and independent assessment mechanisms to ensure energy efficiency standards can be implemented in real operations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, regarding assistance to enterprises, particularly SMEs, in equipment upgrades.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many energy-saving measures require companies to make upfront investments in equipment updates or system optimisation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Large enterprises usually have the resources to carry out these upgrades, but SMEs may face financial and technical constraints.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, even if a SME knows that old equipment consumes more energy, it may not be able to replace it immediately.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As energy systems become increasingly complex, energy management is gradually becoming a field requiring professional skills, including capabilities in data analysis, system optimisation and industrial process management.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, even if businesses purchase efficient equipment, without professional personnel to analyse energy consumption data and optimise operating methods, the equipment's efficiency may not be fully realised.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, I suggest the Government strengthen cooperation between industry and higher education institutions to develop more professional courses in energy efficiency and energy management, to ensure businesses can obtain the talent they need.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Speaker, energy efficiency may not be as eye-catching as new energy technologies, but it remains one of our most direct and cost-effective solutions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Every unit of energy we save means reduced imports, reduced power generation demand, lower costs and reduced carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
